label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
Subject: The building on Saint-Hubert

Denis,

I am going to write this in English so there is no confusion about what I say. I have started this email in French four times and each time it became something I don't want to send. So I am trying again, slowly.

On Thursday morning, at six o'clock, a man with a camera walked into my shop while I was shaping the baguettes. He said he was a photographer for the agency, and that you had told him I was fine with the sale. I had flour on my hands. Karine, who has worked with me for eleven years, had to sit me down and bring me water, because I could not stand up straight. I learned that my brother is selling the building where I have had my bakery for thirty-one years from a stranger, in my own shop, before the bread was even out of the oven.

I found the listing online afterwards. One million one hundred and fifty thousand dollars. I read it three times. I did not believe it, and then I did.

Denis, you did not call me. Not once. You used an agent to tell me, like I was a tenant who didn't pay on time. I have never been late on rent, not one month in all these years. I pay two thousand four hundred dollars a month to the estate for that space, and I paid for the new roof in 2019 myself, thirty-eight thousand dollars, because the building needed it and nobody else was going to pay. I did not ask anyone for credit for that. I did it because it was our papa's building and I wanted it to stay in good shape.

I want to remind you of what I told you in September, on the phone. I told you I wanted to buy your half. The Caisse has already pre-approved me for four hundred and ten thousand dollars. I was careful and I did the work. I did not come to you with a dream, I came with numbers. You said you would think about it. I thought that meant you were considering it with me. I was wrong, I understand that now.

Then, after Maman's funeral, you called me and said, "No rush, we decide together." Together. I remember how you said it, like it was something kind. Together is not something you do with a listing on Centris and a photographer in my shop.

You know what I remember when I think about this building? When we were kids, Papa let you sleep in the room in the back, with the flour sacks, because you loved the smell and the quiet. You would come out in the morning covered in flour, laughing, and I was jealous, I will admit it. I was the one who got up at four to help him, and you were the one who got to sleep there. But I did not mind, because it was ours. The building was the thing that held us together after Papa died, and then after Maman. I think that is why this hurts so much. It is not only about money for me, even if you think I am being sentimental.

It is also about money, and I want you to hear the business side too, because you have never worked in this building. I have six employees. Karine has been with me eleven years. Marc has been with me nine. They are not just names on a payroll, they have families too. I have thirty-one years of clients who come every morning and know my face. If the developer buys this building, and we both know what developers do on Saint-Hubert, they will tear it down or make condos out of it. My rent will double, maybe more, and I will not survive that. I will lose the bakery. Everything Papa built, everything Maman helped with, everything I put into this place for three decades, gone, and the people who work for me gone with it. You know I am not exaggerating. You grew up in this building too.

I am not writing to threaten you. I am writing because I am furious and I want you to understand exactly how furious, but I also do not want to lose you. You are my brother. I am not ready to lose you over a building, and I don't think you want to lose me either, even if this week it does not feel that way.

So here is what I am asking. I need two things from you.

First, take the building off the market this week. Call the agent and tell him to stop. If you can't do that, then at the very least give me the first right to buy your half before anyone else sees it. I am ready to talk about a fair price. I have the financing ready. I am not asking for a gift. I am asking to be treated like the person who has been paying, working, and caring for this place this whole time.

Second, I want you to answer me by phone. Please do not send a text, and please do not have your wife send me a message about it. I love her, and I know she is not the one who made this decision, but this conversation has to be between you and me. I want to hear your voice. I want to hear why you did this and why you did it without telling me first. If you have a reason I have not thought of, I want to hear it. Maybe I am missing something. Maybe you are in trouble, or you need money I don't know about. If that is the case, tell me. Don't let an agent tell me instead.

I know this email sounds angry. I am angry. But I am not writing to hurt you. I am writing because I still believe we can fix this, and because I still remember the boy who slept with the flour sacks and came out laughing. I want that brother back. I want to have a real conversation, not a listing.

Please call me this week. I am available any morning after the bread is out, which is when I am usually free, or in the evening after eight.

I love you, Denis. I need you to understand what this building means to me, and to our family, before anything else gets signed.

[Your name]
